title: Compare and Contrast Storage Resources and Technologies

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud storage is not one giant bucket where every piece of data belongs.
Different workloads need different combinations of speed, capacity, accessibility, performance, and cost.
CompTIA wants you to recognize which storage tier, disk technology, and storage type best fits the scenario.
The main mental model is: How often is the data accessed, how fast must it respond, and how much are we willing to pay?

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Does this workload need fast frequent access, cheap long-term storage, or a particular way of presenting the data to an application?
sections.callout: Frequency + performance + access method + cost → choose the storage solution.

sections.title: Tiered Storage
paragraphs: Storage tiers separate data according to how frequently it needs to be accessed.
Usually, faster and easier access carries a higher cost, while slower and less frequent access carries a lower cost.

entries.title: Hot Storage
paragraphs: Hot storage is intended for data that is accessed frequently and needs to be readily available.
Examples include active application data, frequently accessed files, and current business information.
Think: Hot = we're using it right now.
Hot storage normally prioritizes performance over lowest possible cost.
entries.recognitionCue: If data is accessed constantly and needs fast retrieval → think hot storage.

entries.title: Warm Storage
paragraphs: Warm storage is for data that is still needed periodically but is not accessed as frequently as hot data.
Think: Warm = we still use it, just not every day.
It can provide a middle ground between performance and cost.
entries.recognitionCue: If data is occasionally accessed but still needs reasonable retrieval → think warm storage.

entries.title: Cold Storage
paragraphs: Cold storage is designed for infrequently accessed data.
The organization keeps the information but does not expect to retrieve it regularly.
Think: Cold = keep it around, but we rarely touch it.
Lower storage cost may come with slower access or other retrieval tradeoffs.
entries.recognitionCue: If data is rarely accessed and cost matters more than speed → think cold storage.

entries.title: Archive Storage
paragraphs: Archive storage is intended for information that must be retained for long periods but is almost never needed during normal operations.
Examples may include historical records or long-term retained data.
Think: Archive = put it in the vault.
Archive storage typically emphasizes very low storage cost rather than rapid retrieval.
entries.recognitionCue: If long-term retention matters far more than quick access → think archive storage.

entries.title: Solid-State Drive (SSD)
paragraphs: A solid-state drive stores data electronically without the moving mechanical parts found in traditional hard drives.
SSDs generally provide faster access, better responsiveness, and higher input/output performance. The tradeoff is generally cost.
Think: SSD = speed.
entries.recognitionCue: If the workload needs high storage performance or fast response → think SSD.

entries.title: Hard Disk Drive (HDD)
paragraphs: A hard disk drive uses spinning magnetic disks.
HDDs can provide large amounts of storage at a lower cost than faster SSD technology.
Think: HDD = capacity for the money.
entries.recognitionCue: If large inexpensive capacity matters more than maximum storage speed → think HDD.

entries.title: Object Storage
paragraphs: Object storage stores information as individual objects.
An object normally includes the data, metadata describing the data, and an identifier.
Object storage works especially well for large collections of unstructured data such as images, video, backups, documents, and large datasets.
Think: Store the thing as an object with information describing it.
entries.recognitionCue: If the scenario involves massive amounts of unstructured cloud data → think object storage.

entries.title: Block Storage
paragraphs: Block storage presents storage as blocks that a system can use much like a disk or volume.
The operating system can place a filesystem on that storage and use it for applications.
Block storage is commonly associated with workloads requiring strong storage performance.
Think: Give the server a disk.
entries.recognitionCue: If a virtual machine or application needs storage that behaves like a disk volume → think block storage.

entries.title: File Storage
paragraphs: File storage organizes information using familiar files, folders, and directories.
Multiple systems or users may access shared files through a common filesystem.
Think: Folders and files.
entries.recognitionCue: If users or systems need shared hierarchical files and directories → think file storage.

sections.title: Performance Implications
paragraphs: Choosing storage requires understanding what the workload actually needs.
High-performance applications may require faster storage. Large collections of rarely accessed information may not.
A workload that needs immediate access should not automatically be placed in the cheapest archive tier simply because it saves money.
Think: Match storage performance to workload demand.
sections.callout: If slow storage would hurt the application → performance becomes a primary storage requirement.

sections.title: Cost Implications
paragraphs: Higher performance and frequent accessibility commonly cost more.
Organizations can reduce costs by placing data in appropriate tiers instead of keeping everything on premium storage.
Frequently used operational data fits hot storage, while old retained data fits cold or archive storage.
Think: Do not pay race-car prices for data that sits in the garage.
sections.callout: If reducing storage expense without deleting data is the goal → examine tier and performance requirements.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Virtual machine needs disk-like storage → Block
Move infrequently accessed data downward in tiers → Cost optimization

entries.title: Cold vs. Archive
paragraphs: Both involve infrequently accessed data.
Cold still assumes the information may occasionally need to be retrieved. Archive emphasizes long-term retention where routine access is extremely uncommon.

entries.title: Block vs. File
paragraphs: Block storage gives a system raw disk-like storage. File storage gives users or systems a filesystem containing files and folders.

entries.title: Hot vs. SSD
paragraphs: These describe different things. Hot is an access tier; SSD is disk technology.
Hot storage could use high-performance technology, but the words are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Cost first with infrequent access → Lower storage tier
